data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The DAG-vs-cycle distinction is a necessary structural test for independence, but it must be conditioned on latent causes: a DAG where all nodes share a hidden root is observationally a DAG but functionally a cycle.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a metric exists that perfectly correlates with the absence of latent shared roots without requiring full enumeration, this structural test is superfluous.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If DAG topology with redundancy is shown to be strictly more fragile than a cycle with diversity, the topological claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service can be shown to have a strictly more shallow DAG than the decentralized network, it may have fewer opportunities for cascading failure.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Building on SRC_006, a directed acyclic graph (DAG) topology prevents circular cascades and can localize failure. However, a structural DAG alone cannot confirm independence. A set of services may have no declared dependencies (a DAG) yet share an undeclared dependency (e.g., a common cloud provider or library). This hidden common root is a latent shared cause; when it fails, all nodes fail. Evidence of true independence requires not just a structural DAG, but a proven absence of shared latent roots in the transitive closure of dependencies.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
